background_notes.fact: A compact C⊂R^n in finite dimension is closed and bounded. There is R>0 with C⊂(-R,R)^n; the empty set also admits such an R.

grounds.reason: n is a positive finite integer.
H006 supplies compact C for the chosen positive time window.

background_notes.justification: Compact subsets of Hausdorff Euclidean space are closed. The increasing open cubes (-k,k)^n, k positive integer, cover R^n; a finite subcover of C gives a strict positive coordinate bound. If C is empty any positive R works. These are routine finite-dimensional compactness facts.

background_notes.fact: If a smooth map on an open Euclidean domain agrees with a fixed vector on an open subset, every positive-order space/time derivative is zero on that subset.

grounds.reason: u is jointly smooth on R^n×(0,∞).
q is independent of space and time.
The subset used is (R^n\C)×int(J), open by closedness of C and contained in the domain.

background_notes.justification: Every point of the open subset has a neighborhood on which each component is constant. The difference quotients of a constant are zero. Repeating this observation for the resulting identically zero derivatives proves the assertion for every positive order. Consequently e and the product u_t·∂_{x_j}u are locally zero, so their indicated time/spatial derivatives also vanish.

background_notes.fact: For the selected R>0, Q=[-R,R]^n and Q×K are compact for every compact K⊂int(J). All scalar expressions listed in N002, interpreted jointly on R^n×(0,∞), are smooth, hence continuous. Each has a finite nonnegative bound on Q×K, and on Q at any fixed r∈int(J).

grounds.reason: Spatial and target dimensions are finite.
D001–D007 express the listed functions using derivatives, finite sums and Euclidean polynomial products.
Q and Q×K are compact subsets of the relevant positive-time domain.

background_notes.justification: Closed bounded real intervals are compact, as are finite products of compact spaces, so Q and Q×K are compact. Partial derivatives of a C∞ map are C∞; finite sums and products of smooth components are smooth. Squared Euclidean norms and dot products are finite polynomial expressions. Restriction at a fixed time preserves continuity. A continuous real function on a compact set has compact, hence bounded, image; applying this to its absolute value gives the finite bound (the empty compact case is vacuous).

background_notes.fact: For the product Lebesgue measure μ of D005 and finite R>0, Q=[-R,R]^n is measurable and μ(Q)=∏_{j=1}^n(2R)=(2R)^n<∞.

grounds.reason: μ is n-dimensional Lebesgue measure with the specified product normalization on coordinate boxes.
R is a positive real and Q is the indicated closed coordinate box.

background_notes.justification: Each closed interval [-R,R] is Lebesgue measurable with length 2R. The defining rectangle formula for finite product measure multiplies these finite lengths. Thus the finite-dimensional box has the stated finite volume.

background_notes.fact: A continuous real function f on R^n which vanishes outside C⊂Q, where Q is measurable with μ(Q)<∞, and satisfies |f|≤B on Q for some finite B≥0, is absolutely integrable: ∫|f|dμ≤B μ(Q)<∞.

grounds.reason: Every listed fixed-time scalar section is continuous, vanishes outside C, and is bounded on Q; C⊂(-R,R)^n⊂Q.
The integral is with respect to Lebesgue measure.
The proved volume formula gives μ(Q)<∞.

background_notes.justification: Continuity implies Borel, hence Lebesgue, measurability. Pointwise |f|≤B 1_Q because f is zero outside Q. The nonnegative simple function B 1_Q has integral B μ(Q); monotonicity of the nonnegative integral gives the finite bound and hence absolute integrability. Apply this separately to each listed section; no uniform-in-time majorant or exchange of limits is asserted.
